newsitem.title: MEXICO: FEATURE-Mexico's huge reforms are real story - U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mexico's huge reforms are real story - U.S. envoy.

text.p: His watch included two guerrilla uprisings and an economic near-collapse, but U.S. Ambassador James Jones believes some foreign reporters have missed the biggest story in Mexico in the past four years.

"When I go back to Washington or New York you would think the only thing that's happening in Mexico is drug trafficking, insurrections and high-level corruption," Jones told Reuters in a farewell interview before departing his post. "Clearly that's a story -- but it's not the whole story."

More important than headline-grabbing rebel attacks or tales of drug corruption, he says, are huge political and economic changes that are transforming Mexico's closed economy and one-party political system into a free-market democracy.

Jones, a Democratic congressman from Oklahoma in 1973-87, says "we never even considered Mexico" for most of that period. "It was a non-entity. It was just a closed, protected economy. Then they joined GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) 10 years ago and look what's happened since."

Under free-market reforms that began in 1982 and accelerated sharply under the 1988-94 presidency of Carlos Salinas de Gortari, Mexico privatised, abandoned big-state dogmas, tore down trade barriers and wooed foreign investment.

President Ernesto Zedillo has added political reforms, pushing through bills for direct election of Mexico City's mayor, putting electoral authorities under independent citizen control and giving generous public funding to the opposition. As a result, political analysts say Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled the country for 68 unbroken years, could lose its lower house majority for the first time in congressional elections on July 6.
'LOOK WHAT'S HAPPENED IN FOUR YEARS'
"When I came here the political system was opening but it was not much different than it was in 1930," Jones said.

"Look what's happened in four years. They're not talking about whether the elections will be rigged this time, they're talking about how do we get votes and win an honest election. That's a remarkable thing that's going to have long-term benefits."

Jones took up his post in Mexico in August 1993 and knows Salinas and Zedillo well. He compares Salinas -- famous for his image-polishing skills -- to a "showhorse" while Zedillo is a workhorse, plodding steadily but getting long-term results. As a result, he says, Zedillo has been severely under-estimated in office just as Salinas was over-estimated.

Critics have lampooned Zedillo as a nerdy technocrat who lacks political savvy and communicates poorly but defenders point to his far-reaching reforms, honesty and determination to root out corruption and improve a discredited legal system.

"He's a very private person but he's a very genuine person," Jones said of Zedillo. "Very smart, stubborn many times. Because he is such a private person -- this is my opinion -- it's been difficult for him to communicate as a traditional Latin leader."

But like other Mexico-watchers, Jones says big political and economic reforms do not mean Mexico is guaranteed a safe passage to steady long-term growth and prosperity. His main worry about the future is what he terms the "opportunity gap" -- the large part of the population living in dire poverty who have yet to feel any benefit from the free-market reforms.
TOO MANY FEEL THERE IS NO HOPE
"It's not just Mexico, it is the rest of this hemisphere, Eastern Europe and certain parts of Asia," he said. "You can't have 30, 40, 50 percent of your population feeling that there's no hope."

Jones blames the "opportunity gap" for Mexico's two guerrilla movements -- Zapatista Indian rebels who briefly rose up in January 1994 and Marxist EPR guerrillas who turned up in the poor southwestern state of Guerrero. "As long as you have this opportunity gap problem you will have pockets of violent protest but I don't see anything out there either that exists now or that is contemplated that is destabilising."
Mexico holds elections on July 6 to elect a new lower house of congress, a quarter of the Senate, its first elected mayor of Mexico City and six state governors.

Despite Zedillo's warnings against "false demagogues" who promise to transform life from one day to the next, polls show the leftist opposition are likely to win the symbolically important Mexico City job and Zedillo's party may lose its lower house majority for the first time ever.

But Jones is sanguine about the risks. "The president would have a much easier time getting his programme through relying on his party to supply the majority, but I am not all that disturbed at the prospect that you would have to have ad hoc coalitions," he said.

The reason for his optimism is two-fold: he believes all three of the country's main parties are moving toward the centre and he doubts any opposition party would want to be seen as a wrecker ahead of presidential elections in 2000.
"I think it's going to take more effort for President Zedillo because coalitions are harder to put together ... but I do think that ad hoc coalitions can also be responsible," he said.
